P-Adic Geometries and Processable
Holograms: Theoretical Syntheses and
Photonic Computational Architectures
The Holographic Paradigm in Non-Archimedean
Frameworks

The fundamental architecture of spacetime and the limits of computational processing have
historically been evaluated through the lens of real and complex numbers—fields governed
intrinsically by the Archimedean axiom, which dictates that any magnitude can be exceeded by
adding a smaller magnitude to itself sufficiently many times. However, at the intersection of
high-energy theoretical physics, non-Archimedean mathematics, and next-generation
computational hardware, this continuous paradigm is giving way to hierarchical, discrete
models. Investigations into generic quantum gravity suggest a fundamental breakdown of the
Archimedean axiom at the Planck scale. When the uncertainty of a spatial measurement \Delta
x meets or exceeds the Planck length \ell_P = \sqrt{\hbar G / c^3} \sim 10^{-33} cm, the
underlying geometry cannot be adequately described by smooth, continuous manifolds. At such
scales, the uncertainty of the measuring quantity is not smaller than the value being measured,
necessitating a mathematical framework built upon discrete, fractal topologies.
In response, theoretical physicists have increasingly turned to p-adic mathematical physics,
utilizing the field of p-adic numbers (\mathbb{Q}_p) and their inherent ultrametric topologies to
model spacetime as a hierarchical structure. This transition has birthed the p-adic Anti-de
Sitter/Conformal Field Theory (AdS/CFT) correspondence, a holographic duality where a bulk
gravitational theory situated on a discrete infinite graph—the Bruhat-Tits tree—is dual to a
Conformal Field Theory residing on its boundary. Simultaneously, the concept of holography has
transcended theoretical physics, evolving into a practical, engineering paradigm within computer
science and optics. Processable holograms, enabled by optical computing and spatial light
modulators (SLMs), allow for the real-time manipulation of multidimensional data through the
interference of light waves.
This report provides an exhaustive analysis of both theoretical p-adic simulations and physical
processable holograms. By examining the tensor network formalisms that underpin p-adic
AdS/CFT and mapping them onto the diffractive neural networks that power optical computing,
this analysis reveals a profound structural isomorphism. The physical instantiations of
holographic computing offer a highly analogous architecture to the theoretical tensor networks
used to model p-adic quantum mechanics. Consequently, this synthesis suggests that photonic
hardware, diffractive networks, and magnonic processors could eventually serve as direct
analog simulators for non-Archimedean quantum gravity.
The Mathematical Edifice of Non-Archimedean
Geometry

To comprehend the architecture of p-adic physical models, it is essential to delineate the
foundational mathematics of p-adic numbers. Introduced by Kurt Hensel in 1897, the field of
p-adic numbers \mathbb{Q}_p arises from the completion of the field of rational numbers
\mathbb{Q} with respect to the p-adic norm, rather than the standard Euclidean absolute value
used to construct the real numbers \mathbb{R}.

The P-Adic Norm and Ultrametricity

For any prime number p, any non-zero rational number x can be represented in the form x =
p^\gamma \frac{a}{b}, where a and b are integers not divisible by p, and \gamma is an integer.
The p-adic norm is defined strictly as:
\vert{}x\vert{}_p = p^{-\gamma}, \quad \vert{}0\vert{}_p = 0
Unlike the standard metric on the real numbers, the p-adic metric d_p(x, y) = \vert{}x - y\vert{}_p
satisfies the strong triangle, or ultrametric, inequality:
\vert{}x + y\vert{}_p \leq \max(\vert{}x\vert{}_p, \vert{}y\vert{}_p)
This simple, rigorous modification has profound topological and geometrical consequences. In
an ultrametric space, all triangles are isosceles, every point inside a ball serves equally as its
center, and the space itself is totally disconnected—meaning that open sets can be completely
disjoint while still covering the space. These properties make p-adic numbers intrinsically suited
for modeling systems with a hierarchical, tree-like structure, such as phylogenetic classifications
in biology, the state spaces of spin glasses, and the discrete fractal geometries of quantum
gravity.
A general non-zero p-adic number can be uniquely expressed as a canonical formal series in
powers of p:
x = \sum_{i=\gamma}^{\infty} x_i p^i
where x_i

0. This series converges absolutely with respect to the p-adic norm because the magnitude of
the terms p^i becomes exponentially small as i approaches infinity. The p-adic integers, denoted
\mathbb{Z}_p, consist of sequences where \gamma \geq 0, forming the unit ball of
\mathbb{Q}_p, which geometrically represents an infinite rooted tree with a fractal structure.

Adelic Physics and Number Field Invariance

The interplay between the real and p-adic norms is strictly constrained by the Adelic product
formula, which unifies the Archimedean and non-Archimedean domains. For any non-zero
rational number x \in
\mathbb[span_32](start_span)[span_32](end_span)[span_33](start_span)[span_33](end_span)[
span_34](start_span)[span_34](end_span){Q}, the product of its real norm and all its p-adic
norms equals one:
\vert{}x\vert{}_\infty \prod_p \vert{}x\vert{}_p = 1
This constraint is an expression of the Hasse-Minkowski local-global principle, which posits that
if a mathematical statement holds across all local fields (the real numbers and all p-adic fields),
it inherently holds on the global field of rational numbers. From a theoretical physics
perspective, this implies the existence of a number-field invariance principle: the fundamental
physical laws governing reality should remain invariant regardless of whether they are
formulated over real or p-adic fields. This has driven the development of adelic string theory,

where scattering amplitudes, such as the crossing-symmetric Veneziano amplitude, are
evaluated as products over all p-adic fields to compute full Adelic interactions.
P-Adic Quantum Mechanics and Spectral Theory

In formulating p-adic quantum mechanics, standard physical formalisms built upon the real
continuous line must be fundamentally adapted. Due to the total disconnectedness of
\mathbb{Q}_p, local derivatives do not exist in the traditional continuous sense, as the limit
defining the derivative depends on the direction of approach, which is undefined in an
ultrametric topology. Consequently, there is no direct p-adic equivalent to the traditional
momentum operator p = -i\hbar \nabla acting on a smooth manifold.
Instead, p-adic quantum mechanics is rigorously formulated using the Dirac-von Neumann
axioms via probability measures over the space of generalized functions. The Hilbert space is
established as \mathcal{H} = L^2(\mathbb{Q}_p^N), where wavefunctions map p-adic spatial
coordinates to complex amplitudes. To construct quantum evolution without standard
derivatives, physicists employ the Weyl representation. A pair of unitary operators is defined
using the additive character \chi(x) = \exp(2\pi i \{x\}), where \{x\} represents the fractional part of
x:
U_q: \psi(x) \rightarrow \psi(x + q) V_p: \psi(x) \rightarrow \chi(px) \psi(x)
Because local differential equations—such as the continuous continuous-time Schrödinger
equation—are mathematically invalid over \mathbb{Q}_p, the dynamics are modeled through
pseudodifferential operators, most notably the Vladimirov operator D^\alpha. The action of this
operator on a complex-valued function of a p-adic argument relies on the Fourier transform over
the p-adic space:
D^\alpha f(x) = \int_{\mathbb{Q}_p} \chi(-kx) \vert{}k\vert{}_p^\alpha dk

) d\mu(k)
Alternatively, p-adic quantum dynamics are described through Feynman path integrals. In the
path integral formulation, the evolution operator U(t) for a p-adic harmonic oscillator is derived
by integrating over p-adic trajectories with specific boundary conditions q(0) = y and q(t) = x. A
remarkable feature of this formulation is that the propagator for a massive particle exhibits a
power-law decay at infinity (e.g., proportional to \vert{}t\vert{}_p^{-3}) rather than the exponential
decay observed in Archimedean quantum mechanics.
Furthermore, p-adic wavelets have been developed as eigenvectors of the Vladimirov operator.
The orthonormal basis of p-adic wavelets in L^2(\mathbb{Q}_p) allows for non-Archimedean
multiresolution analysis. Because standard translations by integers are impossible in a totally
disconnected space, these wavelets utilize translations by representatives of the factor group
\mathbb{Q}_p/\mathbb{Z}_p. These unique spectral properties facilitate advanced investigations
into the correlation functions of spin glasses (such as the Parisi matrix parametrization) and
ultrametric continuous-time quantum walks, modeling particles that cannot be precisely
localized due to fractal quantum uncertainties.
Number Theory, Thermodynamics, and Quantum
Spacetime

The hierarchical nature of p-adic quantum mechanics provides a profound mathematical link

between thermodynamics, prime numbers, and the geometry of spacetime. One of the most
critical theoretical bridges is the Bost-Connes system, a quantum statistical model wherein the
partition function Z(\beta) matches the Riemann Zeta function \zeta(\beta), where \beta = 1/kT is
the inverse temperature.
This system undergoes a spontaneous symmetry breaking—a thermodynamic phase
transition—exactly at \beta = 1, corresponding to the pole of the zeta function. In this
non-commutative space of adele classes, the nontrivial zeros of the Riemann zeta function
\gamma_n manifest not as standard emission energy levels, but as an absorption spectrum,
acting as a spectral thermostat for a quantum system built fundamentally from prime numbers.
The interpolation of these functions into the p-adic domain relies on the Kubota-Leopoldt
p[span_63](start_span)[span_63](end_span)-adic L-function L_p(s, \chi), which analytically
continues the complex Dirichlet L-function across the p-adic disk. The Weierstrass preparation
theorem decomposes this function as:
L_p(T, \chi) = p^\mu \cdot P(T) \cdot U(T)
This formulation enforces the Adelic product formula at every layer of the Iwasawa Tower—the
\mathbb{Z}_p-extension of a number field—acting as a non-volatile hierarchical backup log. The
simultaneous processing of the Adelic Handshake ensures synchronization between the p-adic
kernel space and the real user space across observers via the Baum-Connes assembly map.
These arithmetic structures demonstrate that the fundamental fabric of bulk quantum gravity is
indexed by prime numbers, embedding high-energy standard model phenomenology deeply into
the arithmetic of the p-adics.
P-Adic AdS/CFT and the Bruhat-Tits Tree

The most expansive application of p-adic geometry in contemporary theoretical physics is the
p-adic AdS/CFT correspondence. The standard Anti-de Sitter/Conformal Field Theory
correspondence relates a gravitational theory in a continuous d+1-dimensional bulk space to a
conformal field theory on its d-dimensional continuous boundary. In the p-adic formulation, the
continuous bulk geometry is fundamentally replaced by a discrete, infinite graph known as the
Bruhat-Tits tree.

Constructing the Bulk Geometry

The Bruhat-Tits tree, denoted T_p, is an infinite, symmetric, and homogeneous regular graph
with no preferred central vertex. For the field of p-adic numbers \mathbb{Q}_p, every vertex in
the tree has a uniform valency of p+1. Mathematically, this tree is expressed as the left coset
space of the projective general linear group acting on p-adic numbers:
T_p \equiv PGL(2, \mathbb{Q}_p) / PGL(2, \mathbb{Z}_p)
The boundary of this tree at infinity corresponds to the p-adic projective line P^1(\mathbb{Q}_p),
which is equivalent to \mathbb{Q}_p \cup \{\infty\}. Any path extending from the deep bulk of the
tree to the boundary traces out a unique p-adic expansion. Thus, moving inward along the tree
corresponds directly to a coarse-graining of the p-adic number, establishing a perfect geometric
realization of the Renormalization Group (RG) flow.

CFTs on the P-Adic Boundary

A p-adic CFT residing on P^1(\mathbb{Q}_p) shares structural similarities with an Archimedean
CFT but is considerably more analytically tractable due to the lack of descendant fields.
Because continuous functions on \mathbb{Q}_p are locally constant, all derivatives of the
primary fields strictly vanish. The operator product expansion (OPE) is thus exact and heavily
constrained.
When analyzing the OPE in p-adic CFTs, the structure constants C_{ab}^c perfectly define the
fusion rules of the primary operators:
\mathcal{O}_a(x_1) \mathcal{O}_b(x_2) = \sum_c C_{ab}^c \vert{}x_1 - x_2\vert{}_p^{\Delta_c -
\Delta_a - \Delta_b} \mathcal{O}_c(x_2)
These simplifications enable theorists to compute holographic correlators, loop diagrams, and
three-point coefficients for p-adic analogues of structures like the BTZ black hole with an
algebraic precision that is often intractable in standard real-manifold AdS/CFT models.
Holographic Tensor Networks and Emergent Gravity

A critical breakthrough in understanding holography has been the realization that the AdS/CFT
correspondence operates structurally like a tensor network. In the p-adic case, this is not merely
a qualitative analogy; the Euclidean path integral of a p-adic CFT is exactly reproducible by a
tensor network mapping the Bruhat-Tits tree.

Solving the Tensor Map

At each bulk vertex of the BT tree, a (p+1)-valent tensor T^{a_1 \dots a_{p+1}} is placed. These
tensors are constructed entirely from the OPE coefficients C^{abc} and the local bulk
propagators of the p-adic CFT. Unlike previous real-space tensor network proposals (where the
network defined a wavefunction subject to complex quadratic constraints that were difficult to
solve), describing the Euclidean path integral yields linear constraints. This allows the tensor
network configuration for any generic p-adic CFT to be solved explicitly.
For example, in a theory whose structure coefficients match the fusion algebra of the 2D Ising
model, the basis consists of three primary fields: \{\vert{}1\rangle, \vert{}\epsilon\rangle,
\ve[span_95](start_span)[span_95](end_span)rt{}\sigma\rangle\}. The structure constant actions
dictate the tensor contractions, such as C(\sigma)\vert{}\sigma\rangle = \vert{}1\rangle +
\vert{}\epsilon\rangle.
A regularized tree with a cutoff radius \Lambda centered at the origin possesses N = p^\Lambda
(1 + 1/p) boundary edges. The path integral map Z_\Lambda on the regularized tree contracts

the tensors inward from the cutoff boundary. The evolution of the regularized source state
\vert{}J_\Lambda\rangle across radial cutoff levels is governed by the RG flow equation:
\vert{}J_\Lambda\rangle_X = \underbrace{C(G J_{\Lambda+1}) \cdots C(G J_{\Lambda+1})}_{p
\text{ times}} \vert{}1\rangle_X
Any infrared (IR) fixed point of this RG flow satisfies the axioms of a p-adic CFT, with the tensor
operations acting functionally as expectation values of a Wilson line network covering the tree.

Deriving the Graph Einstein Equation

Recent research has successfully derived the emergent graph Einstein equation from these
p-adic CFT tensor networks. By perturbing the boundary conditions of the tensor network away
from the pure conformal fixed point—where every edge has unit length—one induces geometric
fluctuations in the bulk.
If the un-deformed fixed-point boundary vector is V_f^a = \delta^a_1, a perturbation V_{\Lambda
i}^a = \delta_1^a + \lambda v_{\Lambda i}^a is introduced. Contracting these tensors flows the
perturbation into the interior. Researchers parameterize the emergent edge lengths d_e = 1 +
j_e and the local graph curvature R_x as symmetric functions of these flowed vectors.
By defining a covariant bulk matter action S_m^{\text{cov}} coupled to these edge lengths, the
stress tensor T_{xy} and the graph Einstein tensor G_{xy} are derived variationally:
T_{xy} = \frac{\delta S_m^{\text{cov}}}{\delta d_{\langle xy \rangle}}, \quad G_{xy} = \frac{\delta
S_{EH}}{\delta d_{\langle xy \rangle}}
Imposing consistency constraints on the tensor network directly yields the emergent graph
Einstein equation:
G_{xy} + T_{xy} = 0
Solving these equations order-by-order in perturbation parameter \lambda uniquely fixes the
bulk metric, graph curvature definition, and matter-gravity coupling parameters. For instance,
the mass formula m_a^2 = -(p + 1) + p^{1-\Delta_a} + p^{\Delta_a} is naturally extracted,
perfectly reproducing the exact relation required by the discrete Klein-Gordon equation on the
BT tree.
Quantum Error Correction in Holographic Geometries

The stability of these emergent holographic geometries is fundamentally reliant on quantum
error correction (QEC). For the geometry of the bulk to hold together against local perturbations,
the boundary code must maximize information scrambling and entropy across the network.
Holographic tensor-network codes exhibit an algebraic threshold for error correction, where the
error rate scales polynomially rather than exponentially in the thermodynamic limit. Several

The Galois-qudit GRS code is particularly vital for p-adic mechanics, as it facilitates the

physical legs are pre-assigned in these quantum LEGO codes without contracting the logical
legs, the non-local mapping ensures that the destruction of a significant portion of the boundary
CFT data does not erase the deep-bulk quantum states. The global trace formula of an adelic
code ties directly to the prime logs \log p and the lengths of geodesics within the Bruhat-Tits
trees, further entrenching the relationship between number theory and quantum stability.
Computational Architectures for P-Adic Simulations

Translating the abstract mathematics of p-adic non-Archimedean topologies into computable
models presents immense algorithmic challenges. Because a p-adic number requires an infinite
series expansion for exact representation, computational systems must rely on finite precision
truncations and specialized data structures to prevent memory saturation and floating-point
errors.

Specialized Algebra Systems

The algorithmic study of p-adic numbers sits at the frontier of symbolic computation and
numerical analysis. General-purpose programming paradigms fail to handle the ultrametric logic
organically, compelling researchers to utilize specialized computer algebra systems like
PARI/GP and SageMath.
   ●   PARI/GP: Originally designed for fast computations in number theory, PARI/GP is a highly
       specialized C-based system that features built-in types for p-adic numbers, tracking both
       the p-adic valuation and the precision of the sequence simultaneously. The ring of p-adic
       integers \mathbb{Z}_p and the field \mathbb{Q}_p are native primitive constructs. It
       provides distinct modules, such as the thecubic solver, to calculate p-adic polylogarithms.
       However, users must carefully manage precision limitations, particularly when executing
       the highly recursive functional loops required for deep tree-based tensor contractions.
   ●   SageMath: Built on a Python backbone but heavily integrating extensive C/C++ libraries
       (including wrapping PARI natively), SageMath allows for robust, object-oriented handling
       of p-adic fields and finite extensions. It permits researchers to establish polynomial rings
       and multivariable algorithmic structures essential for algebraic geometry over
       \mathbb{Q}_p.

Simulating the Bruhat-Tits Tree and Machine Learning

Simulating the bulk geometry of the Bruhat-Tits tree requires constructing algorithms that can
traverse infinite, (p+1)-valent graphs. In practice, this entails writing object-oriented
programs—often optimized in Julia or C++—that instantiate finite-depth truncations of the tree to
study topological data analysis, semigroups of double cosets, and the spectrum of
non-commutative oscillators resident on the tree. For instance, recent studies utilized C++ to
define integral forms of algebraic groups and mass algorithms to extract supercuspidal
representations of non-split p-adic reductive groups.
Furthermore, the integration of p-adic architectures into machine learning holds enormous
potential. Standard machine learning operates over the field of real numbers \mathbb{R},
utilizing Euclidean or Hilbert vector spaces \mathbb{R}^d. However, researchers have
demonstrated that simple Quillian semantic networks can be represented far more compactly as
p-adic linear networks—a geometric construction mathematically impossible within the field of

reals due to the lack of ultrametric hierarchy. By structuring data p-adically, neural networks can
natively map taxonomic and hierarchical relationships without forced embeddings, accelerating
the learning of complex representations.
The primary computational bottleneck in simulating p-adic AdS/CFT or training p-adic networks
on standard hardware is the exponential scaling of boundary states. As the tree depth \Lambda
increases, the number of tensor indices grows at a rate of \mathcal{O}(p^\Lambda). This
exponential explosion on classical von Neumann architectures necessitates a radical shift
toward physical, analog simulation methods.
Processable Holograms and Optical Computing
Substrates

While theoretical physicists model holography mathematically over ultrametric fields, optical
engineers and computer scientists construct physical, processable holograms. Holographic data
processing leverages the properties of light—specifically phase, amplitude, and interference—to
compute multidimensional transformations at speeds entirely unachievable by standard
electronic silicon computing.

The Architecture of Optical Computing

Optical computing circumvents the severe limitations of electronic processors (such as Joule
heating, capacitance latency, and Von Neumann memory bottlenecks) by utilizing photons for
information transfer and processing. Because photons do not generate resistance-based heat
while traveling through free space or waveguides, optical computing achieves vastly superior
energy efficiency while offering massive parallel processing bandwidths.
At the core of this technology is the processable hologram. Unlike static, read-only display
holograms, processable holograms are dynamically rewritten and utilized as active associative
memories and logic gates. Information is encoded into a laser beam's phase and amplitude
using a Spatial Light Modulator (SLM), which acts as an active, pixelated diffraction mask.
When coherent light passes through this mask, it generates complex wavefronts, such as
optical vortices carrying orbital angular momentum (OAM). The twisted, corkscrew nature of the
OAM phase profile allows engineers to multiplex large bandwidths of data into distinct,
orthogonal states within a single beam, fundamentally increasing the dimensionality of the
signal.

Diffractive Neural Networks and Optically Generated Holograms

A critical advancement in holographic information processing is the integration of deep learning
to rapidly generate processable phase data, replacing the computationally heavy, iterative
algorithms previously used for Computer-Generated Holography (CGH). Diffractive Neural
Networks (DNNs) represent an all-optical physical network where the "neurons" are individual
transmissive or reflective pixels on consecutive diffractive layers.
In an Optically Generated Hologram (OGH) network, the physical model directly computes the
diffractive propagation in free space utilizing optical transformation operators. The intensity of
the reconstructed image at distance z is given by:

where \mathcal{F} denotes the Fourier transform, \phi_H is the modulated holographic phase,
and \lambda is the operating wavelength.
Once the network is trained in silico, the specific physical parameters of the diffractive
modulation layers are solidified. These arrays can subsequently process incoming, unknown
target objects into processable holograms essentially at the speed of light, entirely bypassing
electronic memory fetches and digital algorithmic loops. This results in the generation of
high-resolution (e.g., 4K) holograms in fractions of a second (0.15s), with an extended depth of
focus crucial for AR/VR displays and real-time medical imaging.
Magnonic Holography and Spin-Wave Processors

To surpass the diffraction limit of standard optical wavelengths, researchers are investigating
magnonic holographic memory (MHM) devices. Magnonics utilizes spin-waves—collective
excitations of electron spins in a magnetic lattice—rather than photons, to process data.
Because spin-waves operate at significantly shorter wavelengths than optical light while
maintaining compatibility with conventional nanoscale electronic devices, MHM systems provide
exponentially higher storage densities. In a magnonic holographic processor, waveguide
matrices are lined with spin-wave generating and detecting elements along their edges. The
interference of these spin-waves creates a dynamic, processable interference pattern that acts
as a holographic associative memory, offering a promising substrate for high-density,
specialized task data processing that scales far beyond the limits of visible photonics.
Biological Holographic Processing and Non-Local
Memory

The application of processable holograms and non-Archimedean mathematics extends
profoundly into the study of complex biological systems, particularly regarding models of
memory and neuromorphic cognition.
Theoretical biology models demonstrate that biological systems inherently exhibit a hierarchical,
ultrametric structure best analyzed using p-adic analysis. P-adic mathematical physics has
successfully mapped the degeneracy of the genetic (amino acid) code—demonstrating that the
local constancy of a map of a p-adic argument equates to the code's degeneracy—and modeled
the hierarchical conformational dynamics of proteins in structural biology.
More radically, physicists and neuroscientists have proposed that the human brain operates
fundamentally as a physical holographic processor. In this framework, cognitive functions,
auto-associative memory retrieval, and subjective experiences do not rely solely on discrete,
classical synaptic connections. Instead, they depend on continuous field dynamics and the
macroscopic wave interference of quantum fields within the brain's aqueous structures.

Super-Radiance, Microtubules, and Landauer's Principle

The holographic brain hypothesis suggests that structures like microtubules—and the highly
structured biological water enveloping them—can act as physical substrates for coherent
super-radiance. Water acts as an ultimate light source for inducing coherent lasers and an
ultimate sensor for photons. By recording and erasing information via the interference patterns
of these coherent waves, the neocortex could theoretically store data holographically across

multiple hierarchical layers (V1, V2, etc.).
To evaluate the physical viability of this hypothesis, researchers apply the Landauer principle,
which states that the minimum theoretical energy required to record or erase one bit of
information is E = k_B T \ln 2. At physiological temperatures (T \approx 300 K), this limit is
roughly 26 meV. If the brain utilizes super-radiant visible or near-infrared photons (e.g., \lambda
= 1500 nm, corresponding to energies >1 eV, or visible light at 2.4 eV) for memory encoding, the
energy scale is vastly larger than 26 meV. This comfortably ensures that holographic information
can be recorded with virtually no risk of thermal degradation or noise corruption.
Under this model, the theoretical memory capacity of the human brain skyrockets. While
traditional neuroscience estimates the maximum memory capacity—assuming 1 bit per
synapse—at roughly 30 Terabytes (TB), holographic encoding via short-wavelength coherent
waves yields storage capacities scaling into the Petabyte (PB) range.

Morphological Control Theory and Reservoir Computing

This biological model functions analogously to continuous field reservoir computing. Unlike
standard Boolean logic gates which process discretely, a holographic neuro-matrix relies on
constructive and destructive interference patterns, allowing global field effects to govern
non-local information processing. External input functions (sensory data) act as object waves
that interfere with physiological reference states, imprinting stable memory "holograms" in the
neocortex.
The mathematical control theory used to model these continuous phase density distributions of
charged bosons in cerebrospinal fluid directly mirrors the algorithms used to design artificial
Diffractive Neural Networks for optical CGH. By using damping input functions to achieve
step-function-like distributions of charged bosons, physiological holographic models establish a
one-to-one correspondence between external optical signal transfers and subjective
auto-associative memory retrieval.
Synthesizing Physical Simulators for Quantum Gravity

A robust tertiary insight emerges when synthesizing p-adic AdS/CFT tensor networks with
diffractive neural networks: optical holographic computing architectures act as the precise
physical instantiations of the tensor networks used to model p-adic quantum gravity.
In theoretical p-adic holography, the boundary CFT encodes a discrete bulk space via a tensor
network extending inward along the Bruhat-Tits tree. The OPE constraints operating at the
tensor vertices dictate exactly how boundary information is coarse-grained into the bulk
representation.
Similarly, a physical Diffractive Neural Network (DNN) operates via consecutive layers of spatial
phase modulators. An initial 2D light field (representing the CFT boundary) propagates through
layers of diffraction (representing the bulk). The physical interference patterns between layers
act as the "tensors" that contract the input field into a dense, coarse-grained target hologram at
the focal plane.
The difficulty of simulating ultrametric geometries classically on PARI/GP or SageMath lies in
their fractal, exponential algorithmic divergence \mathcal{O}(p^\Lambda). However, an optical
system multiplexing binary Orbital Angular Momentum (OAM) states naturally represents
layered hierarchical data. If one builds a cascaded array of SLMs where each subsequent layer
represents a radial step deeper into the Bruhat-Tits tree (a physical step in the RG flow), the

propagation of the optical wavefront mathematically mirrors the iterative tensor contractions
Z_\Lambda derived by AdS/CFT theorists.
Because light propagates and interferes simultaneously across the entire 3D spatial array, the
computational complexity barrier is circumvented entirely by optical parallelism. The emergent
graph Einstein equations, which govern bulk metric deformations due to boundary perturbations,
could theoretically be simulated in a laboratory. By observing how modifying the phase
distribution on the input SLM (the p-adic boundary) physically warps the downstream intensity
maxima in the 3D volume of the diffractive network (the bulk), researchers could optically trace
the stress-energy tensor T_{xy} of a simulated quantum spacetime.
Furthermore, the robustness of associative holographic memory in optical computing—where a
scratched hologram still reproduces the full 3D image due to non-local data
